In a month, I mastered my wardrobe, looking professional at my work. And I can say that has increased my quality of life dramatically. (Not to mention my girlfriend loves it)

I'm entering the workforce in a tech field, and while I don't need to wear nice clothes to work, I do note that it is a thing the higher ups, the managers, do. It's not much, just a nice dress shirt, tucked in or not, jeans without holes, and decent shoes not sneakers.

So over the past month, I figured out dress shirts that fit my body type really well, don't hang or billow. Ended up going with 4 on-sale shirts from Hugh and Crye. They'll last me a decade if I treat them right. Great. $160. Once I got that down I got some decent leather shoes. A pair of Florshiems from Amazon. $70. And today I noted my white ankle socks don't look good with the outfit so I got 6 pair of Gold Toe denim colored socks. $19.

I redid my wardrobe over the course of a month, moving from T-shirts, to composing myself right around the top 90% at my work, for around $250. I now look a lot more professional and feel a lot better about myself. 10/10 do recommend for something to do in a month.

So we all know this is a ridiculous premise for learning an entire subject in a month, since that's practically impossible. But we can also agree that this could be a cool idea for brushing up on a topic of a subject. Naturally, in learning a subject, you will need to grasp many topics with varying degrees of complexity and relations to other topics. So it may be a good idea to order these topics in a way that sweeps off easy and non-dependent topics to introduce you to larger, more challenging topics, and we could benefit from some sort of analysis of our comprehension sprinkled through the course of learning this subject.....Does this not sound like any curriculum in any class you've ever taken? A lot cheaper though...If I could go back 6 years, get all my course work and not have to enroll, I wouldn't've thought twice about it.

...Wonder if there's a market for a collaborative curriculum builder with knowledge checks and averaged times. Could even be a branching curriculum to eventually fit everybody's needs. If this hasn't been done and is a good idea, don't take it. I have the copyright.

Edit: Just an additional thought. You don't want to learn anything in 21 days, especially tech skills. I was in a CS-like field and didn't realize until too late that I wanted a full CS career. So I spent a lot of my free time trying to quickly pick up knowledge. It worked as in I have a decent job now, but I feel like I missed a lot of core concepts that slow me down in my day-to-day development. I know it's enticing to want to know everything you need now, but it takes a lot of time and effort. Just keep reminding yourself that the benefits are worth it, since the tech industry in a way does not have a ceiling. Lynda is a great resource, I'm finding. The only thing better is actual field experience.
